neighbours.label: the comma right after a conjunction that opens an interpolated phrase ('and, in consequence,' / 'nor, indeed,') in formal nineteenth-century prose
fire: The committee examined the accounts with great care, and, in consequence, several errors were brought to light.
The honourable member rose at a late hour, and, with considerable warmth, opposed the second reading of the bill.
He possessed neither fortune nor connexions, nor, indeed, any of those advantages which commonly secure advancement.
The garrison had been reduced by sickness, and, as a natural result, the works were but feebly defended.
The proprietors declined the proposal, but, upon further reflection, consented to receive a deputation.
The harvest of that year proved deficient, and, in consequence, the price of corn rose to an unusual height.
His lordship received the intelligence with composure, and, without further delay, ordered the regiment to advance.
The treaty was at length concluded, and, to the general satisfaction, the troops were withdrawn from the frontier.
quiet: The committee examined the accounts with great care and brought several errors to light.
The honourable member rose at a late hour and warmly opposed the second reading of the bill.
He possessed neither fortune nor connexions nor any of those advantages which commonly secure advancement.
The garrison had been reduced by sickness and the works were but feebly defended.
The proprietors declined the proposal but afterwards consented to receive a deputation.
The harvest of that year proved deficient and the price of corn rose to an unusual height.
His lordship received the intelligence with composure and ordered the regiment to advance.
The treaty was at length concluded and the troops were withdrawn from the frontier.
